title: Sirimon, Naro Moru or Chogoria? Planning Your First Mt Kenya Hike to Point Lenana

content:
Four days, one main trekking summit and a 2:00am start: that is Mt Kenya hiking for most first-timers. The usual goal is Point Lenana (4,985 m), reached without ropes on the Sirimon, Naro Moru or Chogoria routes with a licensed guide. The drier windows of January-February and July-September give the best odds of a clear summit.

Planning Mt Kenya hiking from Nairobi throws up the same handful of questions every time. Which route suits a first attempt? How many days are enough to acclimatise? How cold is the top, and what happens if the rains arrive early? Below you will find route-by-route stages with camp altitudes, two sample itineraries, a month-by-month weather table, training hikes close to the city and the kit that matters most on summit night.

Quick Facts: Mt Kenya Hiking

  • Trekking summit: Point Lenana, 4,985 m, the highest point on the mountain you can reach without technical climbing
  • Technical peaks: Batian (5,199 m) and Nelion (5,188 m) need rock and ice climbing skills
  • Main routes: Sirimon (north-west), Naro Moru (west) and Chogoria (east), with Burguret as a quieter fourth option
  • Typical Mt Kenya hiking trip: 4-5 days, often climbing one route and descending another
  • Best months: January-February and July-September; long rains roughly March-May, short rains roughly October-December
  • Protected area: Mt Kenya National Park (about 718 sq km, created in 1949), managed by Kenya Wildlife Service and on UNESCO's World Heritage List since 1997

Where Is Mt Kenya and How Do You Get There From Nairobi?

Mt Kenya rises in central Kenya just south of the equator, and its route gates sit near the towns of Nanyuki, Naro Moru and Chogoria. From Nairobi, expect roughly 3-4 hours by road to the western and northern gates and a little longer to Chogoria on the eastern side.

The mountain is a long-extinct volcano whose slopes spill into several counties, including Nyeri, Meru, Laikipia, Tharaka Nithi, Embu and Kirinyaga. Its upper slopes form the national park, while the forest belt below is managed as forest reserve. Most Mt Kenya hiking groups drive north on the Thika Superhighway, then continue through Karatina and Nyeri for the western routes or swing east through Embu for Chogoria.

Can you reach the gates by public transport?

Yes, as far as the nearest town. Matatus and shuttles run from Nairobi to Nanyuki and Naro Moru, and to Chogoria along the Embu-Meru road. The final stretch to the park gate needs a vehicle: Sirimon Gate lies about 15 km east of Nanyuki on the ring road plus a further 10 km of track, and on Chogoria the forest track to the park gate runs for about 32 km. Organised trips almost always include the transfer, which saves a lot of hassle on day one.

Which Mt Kenya Hiking Route Should You Choose?

Choose Sirimon for the gentlest gradient and the best acclimatisation, Naro Moru for the shortest approach, and Chogoria for the finest scenery. A popular compromise is a traverse: up Chogoria for the views, down Sirimon for an easy exit to Nanyuki.

RouteStart and gate altitudeMain camps (approx. altitude)Best for
SirimonNear Nanyuki; Sirimon Gate about 2,650 mOld Moses (3,300-3,400 m), Shipton's Camp (about 4,200 m)First-timers who want a gradual climb on the drier side
Naro MoruNaro Moru town; Met Station roadhead about 3,050 mMet Station, Mackinder's Camp (about 4,200 m)Hikers short on time who acclimatise well
ChogoriaChogoria town; park gate area about 2,950-3,000 mRoad Head (about 3,300 m), Lake Ellis (about 3,650 m), Hall Tarns/Minto's (about 4,290 m)Scenery: Gorges Valley, Lake Michaelson, tarns
BurguretGathiuru, near NanyukiFollows the North Burguret River to Hut TarnExperienced groups wanting solitude

Sirimon: the gradual north-western climb

Sirimon starts at about 2,650 m, where bandas sit just inside the gate, and climbs through forest into giant heather to Old Moses Camp at the end of the track. From there the path crosses tussock moorland with cabbage groundsels before following the ridge above the Mackinder Valley, past scattered giant lobelias, to Shipton's Camp beneath the north faces of Batian and Nelion. The steady gain makes Sirimon the route most first-timers pick for Mt Kenya hiking, and an optional night at Liki North (about 3,990 m) adds an extra acclimatisation stop.

Naro Moru: short, steep and famous for its bog

Naro Moru starts in Naro Moru town, passes the park headquarters and reaches the Met Station at about 3,050 m, a point you can drive to in the dry season. Above it lies the notorious vertical bog, a stretch of wet, tussocky ground that can swallow boots in the rains. The path then drops into the Teleki Valley to Mackinder's Camp at about 4,200 m. Naro Moru is often done as a three-day Mt Kenya hiking trip, which leaves little time for your body to adjust.

Chogoria: the scenic eastern side

For many, Chogoria is the most beautiful Mt Kenya hiking route. It climbs the wetter eastern flank through rosewood forest hung with lichen and a tall bamboo belt, with a side trip to Lake Ellis possible near the top of the forest. Higher up, a ridge walk looks straight down into the Gorges Valley and Lake Michaelson, and the Hall Tarns sit beside the path above a cliff of about 200 m. Water at the tarns has no outflow, so boil or filter it. The rough approach road can turn to deep mud in the rains.

What about Burguret, Timau and Kamweti?

Burguret starts at Gathiuru and is managed with the local community forest association, and it has no bamboo zone on that side. Timau and Kamweti are restricted routes that need permission from Kenya Wildlife Service. These quieter Mt Kenya hiking lines suit experienced groups with a guide who knows them well, not a first climb.

What is the Mt Kenya Summit Circuit?

The Summit Circuit is a trail of about 10 km that loops around the central peaks, joining the main routes at camps such as Shipton's, Mackinder's and Minto's. The loop involves more than 2,000 m of combined ascent and descent and usually takes 2-3 days. Walking part of it is the classic way to link one route up with another route down.

What Does a Typical Mt Kenya Hiking Itinerary Look Like?

A typical itinerary takes four days on Sirimon or five on a Chogoria-Sirimon traverse. Both build up to a high camp at about 4,200-4,300 m, start the summit push around 2:00-3:00am, reach Point Lenana near sunrise and then descend the same day.

The tables below are sample Mt Kenya hiking plans, not fixed schedules. Hours vary with pace, weather and group size, and your guide will adjust them on the mountain.

Sample 4-day Sirimon itinerary

DayStart → endAltitude at endApprox. hours
1Sirimon Gate (2,650 m) → Old Moses Camp, about 9 km3,300-3,400 m3-4
2Old Moses → Shipton's Camp via the Mackinder ValleyAbout 4,200 m6-7
3Shipton's → Point Lenana (4,985 m) → down to Shipton's or Old Moses3,300-4,200 m8-11 in total
4Old Moses → Sirimon Gate → transfer to Nanyuki or Nairobi2,650 m2-3 walking

Sample 5-day Chogoria up, Sirimon down

DayStart → endAltitude at endDistance and hours
1Chogoria forest → park gate bandasAbout 2,950 mAbout 16 km, 4 hours
2Bandas → Road Head → Lake Ellis campAbout 3,650 mAbout 13 km, 5 hours
3Lake Ellis → Minto's area / Hall TarnsAbout 4,290 mAbout 12 km, 4-5 hours
4Summit start about 2:00am → Point Lenana → Shipton's → Old Moses3,300-3,400 mLenana around 6:30am, then about 6 hours down
5Old Moses → Sirimon Gate → Nanyuki → Nairobi2,650 m2-3 hours walking

Notice how long summit day is on both Mt Kenya hiking plans. Climbers who add a rest or acclimatisation day at Shipton's or Minto's usually enjoy the top far more, and the extra night costs little compared with the effort of getting to the mountain from Nairobi in the first place.

When Is the Best Time to Go?

January-February and July-September are the best months for Mt Kenya hiking. The long rains (roughly March-May) and short rains (roughly October-December) bring heavy mud on the lower slopes, mist that hides the peaks and fresh snow higher up.

MonthsTypical conditionsVerdict for Mt Kenya hiking
January-FebruaryDriest and clearest spell; frosty nights at high campPeak season
March-MayLong rains; bog and forest tracks very wet, snow possible near the summitHard going; experienced groups only
JuneRains easing, cool and often cloudyFair
July-SeptemberDry and cold, generally good visibilitySecond peak season
October-DecemberShort rains; afternoon showers and mistPossible with full rain kit

Even in the best Mt Kenya hiking months the mountain makes its own weather. Mornings are usually clear and cloud builds by early afternoon, which is one more reason to start walking early each day. If you climb in the short rains, a good pair of waterproof leg gaiters keeps bog water out of your boots on Naro Moru and the Chogoria forest track.

How Hard Is Mt Kenya Hiking for Beginners?

Point Lenana is a non-technical summit, so a fit beginner can reach it, but the trek is hard. Thin air above 4,000 m, walking days of 6-8 hours and a freezing pre-dawn climb on loose scree are what make it tough, not climbing skill.

The final section to Lenana is steep and can be icy, and the descent on tired legs is where many slips happen. Batian and Nelion are a different undertaking altogether: technical rock and ice climbs that need ropes, experience and a specialist guide. For most people, Mt Kenya hiking means Lenana and the circuit around it.

How do you avoid altitude sickness on Mt Kenya?

Ascend gradually, choose a five-day plan, drink steadily and walk slowly. Headache, nausea, dizziness and unusual tiredness are the warning signs, and if they get worse the answer is to go down.

Altitude sickness can affect anyone above about 2,500 m, whatever their fitness, and a fast Naro Moru ascent gives the body less time to adjust than Sirimon. The NHS has a clear overview of altitude sickness symptoms and prevention. Speak to a doctor before the trip if you have any health concerns or take regular medication.

What happens on summit night?

Summit night, the hardest part of Mt Kenya hiking, starts with a wake-up around 1:30-2:30am, tea and biscuits, and a slow climb by headlamp up switchbacks of scree and rock. Temperatures sit below freezing and wind often makes it feel colder. Groups usually reach Lenana for sunrise, around 6:00-6:30am, after roughly 3-4 hours of walking, then spend 15-20 minutes on top before heading down while the ground is still frozen and firm.

How should you train for it from Nairobi?

Give yourself six to eight weeks of training before a Mt Kenya hiking trip, building to back-to-back days of six hours or more with a loaded daypack. Hill training close to the city prepares your legs and lets you test boots and layers before the real thing.

The crater rim covered in our Mt Longonot hike guide is ideal for steep loose ground, and the long, muddy forest climb in the Elephant Hill hike guide is the closest day-hike match for Mt Kenya's lower slopes. For weekend leg work, the seven-peak ridge of the Ngong Hills hike is under an hour from the city. Our guided day hikes near Nairobi are a sociable way to clock those training hours, and the best hikes in Kenya list has more options sorted by effort.

What Gear Do You Need for Mt Kenya Hiking?

Pack for cold and wet: broken-in waterproof boots, wool socks, a base layer, fleece, insulated jacket, waterproof shell and rain pants, two pairs of gloves, a warm hat, a headlamp and water bottles. Add a warm sleeping bag if your operator does not supply one.

Our day-by-day what to pack for hiking Mt Kenya checklist lists every item, and the companion guide to buying Mt Kenya gear in Nairobi explains how to choose each piece, working back from summit night. If Kilimanjaro is next, the Kilimanjaro gear checklist shows what carries over.

Which items matter most for Mt Kenya hiking?

The kit that matters most is whatever keeps you warm and dry between 2:00am and sunrise:

  • Boots: waterproof, ankle-supporting boots such as the Lowa Renegade Evo GTX Mid, broken in on at least three day hikes first.
  • Socks: three or four pairs of merino wool hiking socks, with one dry pair kept only for sleeping.
  • Hands: thin liners plus insulated, waterproof gloves such as Thinsulate waterproof hiking gloves.
  • Head and face: a warm hat or a fleece-lined balaclava for the wind on the final ridge.
  • Light: a waterproof rechargeable headlamp, charged the night before and kept in an inside pocket.
  • Legs: waterproof over-trousers and one or two foldable trekking poles for the scree descent.

Much of this can be bought as quality thrifted gear, which makes a full set for Mt Kenya hiking far more affordable than buying everything new, and we stock some new items too. You can try on boots, jackets and gloves at the Mountain Mall gear shop near Garden Estate, Shop D39 on the third floor along Thika Road, open Monday to Friday 8:30am-6:00pm and Saturday 9:00am-2:00pm.

Which gear mistakes cause the most trouble?

New boots worn for the first time on day one of Mt Kenya hiking cause more blisters than any trail. Cotton T-shirts and jeans stay wet and cold once the mist rolls in at Old Moses. Headlamp batteries left in a cold outer pocket die halfway up the scree. And a single thick jacket is harder to manage than thin layers, because you overheat on the forest climb and freeze at camp. Our post on layering for cold weather hikes shows how to build a system instead.

Do You Need a Guide and Park Permits for Mt Kenya Hiking?

Plan to climb with a licensed guide or a reputable operator, and pay park entry fees to Kenya Wildlife Service. Fees, camping charges and guide rules change, so confirm current details with KWS before you travel.

A guide finds the route in thick mist, watches for altitude sickness and handles registration at the gate, while porters and cooks carry the heavy loads on most organised Mt Kenya hiking trips. Kenya Wildlife Service publishes park details on its Mt Kenya National Park page; check fees and current rules there or with the park office before you book.

What are the rules inside the national park?

Mt Kenya hiking rules are simple: register at the gate, stay on marked routes, camp only at designated sites and carry out all rubbish. Kenya bans single-use plastic bags, and plastic bottles and similar items are not allowed in protected areas, so bring refillable bottles and dry bags. Do not feed the hyraxes and birds that hang around the high camps.

Pro Tips for Mt Kenya Hiking

  • Go pole pole: walking slowly, slowly is the best defence against altitude sickness
  • Drink early: sip water through the day rather than gulping a litre at camp
  • Pack dry: keep your sleeping bag and warm jacket in dry bags, even in February
  • Warm batteries: carry phone and headlamp batteries in an inside pocket on summit night
  • Add a day: an extra night at a high camp makes Mt Kenya hiking safer and improves your chance of a clear summit
  • Mind the sun: equatorial sun at altitude burns fast, so use sunscreen, lip balm and sunglasses

What Will You See on the Way Up?

A Mt Kenya hiking trip passes through clear vegetation bands: montane forest from about 1,800 m, bamboo on some routes from roughly 2,400 m, giant heather, then open moorland with giant groundsels and lobelias, and finally bare rock, small glaciers and tarns beneath the main peaks.

The forest is home to monkeys, and buffalo and elephants range through parts of it, so keep together and follow your guide's instructions. On the moorland, rock hyraxes, sunbirds and alpine chats are common around the camps. Above about 4,600 m only mosses and lichens survive. The Lewis and Tyndall glaciers are the largest of the mountain's small, shrinking ice fields, and the view from Lenana stretches across the Laikipia plateau towards the Aberdares. You can read more on the mountain's zones in Britannica's Mount Kenya entry.

Mistakes That Stop People Reaching Point Lenana

Most Mt Kenya hiking attempts that fall short of Lenana come down to pace, sleep and cold rather than fitness. Rushing the first two days, skipping meals at altitude and arriving at high camp soaked are the usual culprits.

  1. Booking a three-day Mt Kenya hiking trip to save time, then feeling too unwell at 4,200 m to start the summit push.
  2. Walking at a city pace on day one. The forest section feels easy, but it is where you set yourself up for the altitude.
  3. Not eating. Appetite drops above 3,500 m, yet summit night needs fuel, so carry snacks you actually like.
  4. Letting your sleeping layers get damp. Wet clothes at camp mean a cold, sleepless night before the hardest day.
  5. Ignoring early headache or nausea. Tell your guide straight away; an early decision keeps the whole group safer.

None of these need special skills to fix. They need a slower plan, a little discipline and gear that keeps you dry, which is why the same advice comes up again and again from people who have done the climb.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do I need for Mt Kenya hiking?

Hiking Mt Kenya to Point Lenana usually takes four to five days. Fast Naro Moru plans squeeze it into three days, but they give your body little time to adjust to altitude. A five-day trip, such as up Chogoria and down Sirimon, improves acclimatisation and gives you a better chance of a clear, enjoyable sunrise on the summit.

Can I climb Mt Kenya with no hiking experience?

You can climb Mt Kenya to Point Lenana without previous mountain experience, because the route needs no ropes, but you should not arrive untrained. Spend six to eight weeks on regular hill walks near Nairobi, pick a five-day itinerary, go with a licensed guide and pack proper cold-weather gear. Batian and Nelion are technical climbs and not for beginners.

How cold does it get at the top of Mt Kenya?

The top of Mt Kenya is below freezing at dawn, when most hikers reach Point Lenana, and wind on the final ridge makes it feel colder still. Nights at the high camps around 4,200 m are also near or below freezing. An insulated jacket, waterproof shell, warm hat or balaclava and insulated gloves are needed for summit night.

Is Mt Kenya harder than Kilimanjaro?

Mt Kenya's trekking summit, Point Lenana at 4,985 m, is lower than Kilimanjaro's Uhuru Peak at 5,895 m, so the altitude is less extreme. However, Mt Kenya hiking routes are often wetter, boggier and rougher underfoot, and its itineraries are shorter, leaving less time to acclimatise. Many hikers find the two mountains demanding in different ways.

Is Mt Kenya hiking possible in the rainy season?

You can hike Mt Kenya in the rainy season, but expect deep mud in the forest, a flooded vertical bog on Naro Moru, mist that hides the peaks and possible snow near Point Lenana. Climbing in the long rains of March-May is hard going. In the short rains, a good guide, full waterproofs, gaiters and dry bags make a summit realistic.

Final Thoughts

Pick your route for how you acclimatise, not for how quickly you can get home. Sirimon gives the gentlest climb, Chogoria the best views and Naro Moru the shortest approach, and five days on any of them beats four. Mt Kenya hiking rewards patience, a dry-season date and layers that stay dry until sunrise on Lenana.

Start with a long hill day near Nairobi this weekend, wear the boots you plan to climb in, and note what felt cold or wet. Then come and fill those gaps with quality thrifted kit before you book your Mt Kenya hiking dates.
